rv.q: This is a meticulous and artfully conceived blend of storytelling, technology and actorly skill, running a tight 90 minutes.
This is a good, old-fashioned ghost-train of a story.

It’s a pretty damn dazzling use of the space. I think if it were to go into the main house then you might ask harder questions of Armitage’s script, which is a fun meta tribute to the classic haunted house ghost story and to the world of audio actors, but maybe feels a little too much like an extended episode of Inside No 9 for its own good.
In any good rollercoaster ride, the achingly slow rise is at least as important as the 100mph hurtle that follows.
It's expertly atmospheric – a masterclass in staging horror slickly – and fortunately, its trappings are enough to excuse the slightly naff and overly familiar story.

But not having been made aware prior to showing up for the recording what the story is about, George begins to find the tale genuinely horrifying, and with good reason. What those good reasons are, alas, would be giving away too much.
Whether or not you believe in ghosts, this should prove at the very least a decent work out for your adrenal gland.
a bold, atmospheric piece that redefines how we experience theatre
Writer and director Jamie Armitage brings everything to a pleasing completion without over-explaining the mechanics.

The ghost story within the ghost story is a clever framing device. The modern space of the sound booth, with all its high-tech equipment, sits in complete contrast to the setting of the story about to be told.
A Ghost In Your Ear dials up the scare factor in a way I have never seen in a theatre before.

Put another way, when George chucks jangly keys to Sid past the dummy head, we feel the audio zoom across our headspace, and it’s extraordinary. Over the course of the 90-minute production, we see Blagden twist the head, stroke it, detach it and more to draw us in closer.

The audience I saw the show with was mixed in every way - great to see for Hampstead Theatre - and clearly had a ball with plenty of nervous laughter, whooping and jumps. A distant relative of Inside Number 9, A Ghost In Your Ear is a good old fashioned story which encourages careful viewing and listening to deliver a very, very satisfying outcome.
